vignette:
She is thirty-seven, a musician who has been playing piano since she was six and guitar since fourteen. She lives with her partner of five years in a house with a small recording studio in the basement. For most of her adult life, she has made a living as a session player and occasional performer in small venues around the city. The trauma happened two years ago, during a summer evening show at an outdoor amphitheater. She was on stage, playing rhythm guitar for a local indie band. The crowd was sparse, maybe two hundred people. Halfway through the third song, a bomb hidden in a trash can near the soundboard detonated.

She remembers the sound as a physical force-a blow to the chest that knocked her off balance. The stage lights went out. There was smoke and screaming. She dropped her guitar and fell to her knees, hands over her ears, unable to move. Someone pulled her off stage by her arm. She has no memory of the next hour. Later, she learned that four people died and dozens were injured. She was not physically hurt, but her guitar was destroyed-splintered by shrapnel.

For the first three months after the attack, she could not play music at all. She would sit at the piano, hands hovering above the keys, and feel nothing but a hollow dread. The sound of any sudden noise-a door slamming, a car backfiring-would send her heart racing. She stopped leaving the house except for necessities. Her partner tried to be patient, but there were arguments. She would say she was fine, then spend hours staring at the ceiling.

Now, two years later, she is back to playing, but it is different. She practices alone in the basement studio, always with the door locked. She cannot tolerate an audience. Even a single person listening makes her feel trapped, exposed. She still takes session work when she can-recording parts in isolation, sending files electronically. But she has turned down every live performance offer since the attack. She tells herself she will eventually return to the stage, but she does not believe it.

Her symptoms come in waves. Certain sounds trigger her: the sharp clang of a dropped pan in the kitchen, the rumble of a passing truck, even the hiss of a soda can opening. When this happens, her breath catches and she freezes, scanning the room for an exit. She avoids concerts, crowded restaurants, public transit. She has not been to a grocery store in months-her partner does the shopping.

She also struggles with sleep. Most nights she lies awake, replaying the blast in her mind. She sees the flash of light, feels the vibration in her chest. Sometimes she dreams of running but her legs will not move. She wakes gasping, heart pounding, and cannot fall back asleep. Her partner has learned to sleep on the couch on those nights, though they both pretend it is because he snores.

The worst part, she says, is the numbness. She used to feel music in her body-a vibration, a pulse, a joy. Now she feels only the mechanical pressing of keys and plucking of strings. She can play technically well, but the emotion is gone. She sometimes wonders if she is still a musician at all, or just someone who used to be one.

She feels distant from her partner. He tries to understand, but his sympathy feels like pressure. When he asks how she is, she says "okay," because the truth is too heavy. She has stopped telling him about the flashbacks, the nightmares, the way her hands shake when she hears a balloon pop. She feels alone, even when he is holding her.

She finds some relief in routine: her morning coffee, the familiar weight of her guitar strap, the repetitive scales she plays to warm up. But the relief never lasts. Every day she carries the memory of that night. Every day she hopes the next will be different.
